ExplanationParts.CorpusEarnedOpening: The records describe masters’ work as knocking cangues and breaking locks, often beside pulling wedges and nails or releasing bonds. Mi’an also says two people can do this while not even dreaming of the Buddha teaching.
EvidenceBody: The records place cangues and locks beside release, extraction, or liberating work, so the phrase denotes intervention against bondage.

DraftEvidence.ZenBend: Hanxiu pairs the work with pulling wedges and nails; Feiyin with releasing bonds; Juelang with reviving the dead; Mi’an concedes the skill to two people yet withholds the Buddha teaching.
DraftEvidence.CounterexampleOrLimit: The phrase does not carry a uniformly positive verdict: its prison-breaking work may be granted while its performers are still criticized.

ComparedThings: to break open cangues and smash locks
DifferentThingTest.Reason: The records place cangues and locks beside release, extraction, or liberating work, so the phrase denotes intervention against bondage.

DraftEvidence.AliasRationale: “Knock cangues and break locks” retains both prison implements and the two forceful actions repeatedly paired with releasing or extracting.

ModifierControls.Finding: References to only a cangue or only a lock omit the paired implements of the attested work formula.

FamilyControls.Term: 拔楔抽釘 and 解粘去縛
FamilyControls.Finding: Pulling wedges or releasing bonds often accompanies the phrase, but those neighboring release formulas are not its lexical occurrences.
